youtube.title: You'll Love the GTA 6 Song You Hate. Here's Why #Shorts
youtube.description:
Kai hated this song on Monday. By Friday, he's singing it.

GTA 6 launch week: Kotaku counted 150 songs on just the game's pop and classic rock radio stations. But one track keeps coming back, and Kai doesn't switch it off. What changed? Not the song. Just how often he heard it.

In 1968, psychologist Robert Zajonc showed people strange words and symbols 0, 1, 2, 5, 10 or 25 times. The more often people saw one, the more they tended to like it: the mere exposure effect. Familiar feels safe, and safe feels good. Music works the same way, up to a point: in later studies, liking for songs rose with the first few plays and fell again after too many (an inverted U). Like a joke: funny the second time, annoying the tenth.

So, which song did you hate, then love?

Sources:
- Kotaku (2026-11-19), GTA 6's pop and classic rock radio stations contain 150 songs (count attributed): https://kotaku.com/gta-6s-pop-and-classic-rock-radio-stations-contain-150-songs-more-than-all-of-vice-citys-radio-stations-combined-2000758551
- Zajonc (1968), Attitudinal effects of mere exposure, JPSP Monograph Suppl. 9(2): https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/22362/1/0000808.pdf
- Szpunar, Schellenberg & Pliner (2004), Liking and memory for musical stimuli as a function of exposure, JEP:LMC: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14979811/
- Schellenberg, Peretz & Vieillard (2008), Liking for happy- and sad-sounding music: https://sites.utm.utoronto.ca/sites/sites.utm.utoronto.ca.glenn_website/files/download/SP&V2008.pdf
- Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mere-exposure_effect

No real songs, titles or artists are named or played in this video; all music and visuals are original.
